newsitem.title: UK: Vote experts predict clear majority for UK Labour.
newsitem.headline: Vote experts predict clear majority for UK Labour.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour party will win a comfortable majority at the next general election because voters are fed up with the ruling Conservatives and their handling of the economy, a Reuters panel of voting experts predicted on Thursday.

Just one of 20 psephologists and professional pollsters questioned by Reuters earlier this week thinks the "Tory" party, hit by allegations of sleaze and divided over Europe, will win a fifth term in office when its mandate expires by next May.

"The electorate believes two things. That the Conservatives are neither competent nor trustworthy and that the Labour party no longer frightens them," said Ivor Crewe, vice-chancellor at Essex University.
Crewe sees a Labour majority of 61 seats in the 659-seat parliament, or a 42 percent share of the vote. The winning party must capture around 330 seats for a clear victory.
The averages of 20 estimates in the survey point to Labour seizing 41.6 percent of the vote, leaving the Conservatives with 36.7 percent, their smallest share in any election since 1979.
The overall prediction for the opposition Liberal Democrats is 16.6 percent.

In a new lower house of parliament expanded by nine seats because of constituency boundary changes, these overall predictions would translate into 346 seats for Labour and 261 for the Conservatives. The Liberal Democrats would get 25 and other parties 27.

The Reuters survey results fit with the overall trend of opinion polls among potential voters. A poll by Gallup for the Daily Telegraph earlier this week gave Labour 54 percent support and the Conservatives 27 percent.
The experts believed Prime Minister John Major would hold out to the last minute to call the election, 16 citing May as the most likely date and four looking to April.

"The writing has been on the wall for this government for four years," said University of Stirling professor John Curtice, whose forecast of a 125-seat majority for Tony Blair's Labour party was the most bullish of those polled.

Of all 19 forecasts for the size of a Labour majority the median -- the middle of all predictions ranked in order -- was for 35 seats and the lowest, predicted by two people, for a five-seat majority.

The results were the first in a series of Reuters surveys leading up to the UK election. Each month 20 leading experts in British voting patterns will be canvassed for predictions of the parties' share of the vote and expected number of seats.

The one prediction of a Conservative win came from David Carlton, Lecturer in International Studies at Warwick University, who was one of the few experts to predict correctly that John Major would win last time in 1992.

"Ever since 1979 the Tory vote has been a static 42 or 43 percent, and I think that is the rock bottom vote for them," Carlton said. Sticking to his guns, he forecast a nine-seat Conservative majority, or 43 percent of the votes, in 1997.
Some analysts noted that evidence of a growing economy, bringing back some signs of a "feelgood factor" the Conservatives desperately want, could work in their favour.

"But this will not be enough to offset the fundamental change in perceptions," warned journalist and independent political analyst Peter Kellner, who gave Blair the credit for shedding Labour of its union-dominated, tax and spend image of the 1970s.

Blair this week set out his election goals to a Labour party conference, promising to boost spending on education and improve patient care while keeping a lid on government spending and inflation and keeping his promises on tax.

"Through the 1980s there was always a surpressed appetite for the kind of politics Tony Blair represents...now Labour is seen as a competent party whose values are in tune with those of most voters," said Kellner.
Frequently in the survey, job insecurity and unemployment were mentioned as the dominant issue for voters.
Asked what would preoccupy the electorate most on voting day, the party likely to run the economy most competently came out on top.

Voters were no longer sure the Conservatives could deliver their promises on the economy, the panel said, after experiences such as tax rises shortly after the 1992 election and Britain's exit from the European Monetary System.

"The only people who believe the Conservatives will win the next general election are certain Labour activists who can't quite believe that Labour will win -- and one Conservative, John Major," said Essex University's Crewe.
